newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain deficit must shrink faster to hit targets.
newsitem.headline: Spain deficit must shrink faster to hit targets.

text.p: Spain remains far from its 1996 target for the central government budget deficit despite a sharp narrowing in September, analysts said on Wednesday.
The Economy Ministry confirmed today that the monthly budget deficit fell 41 pct in September from a year ago and declined 13.2 percent in the first nine months of the year.

But the decline was still insufficient to ensure that the central government cut its deficit to 3.5 percent of gross domestic product this year as it would have to decline by over 16 percent in the whole 1996, analysts said.
The overall budget deficit goal for 1996, including Social Security, certain public firms and regional and local communities, is 4.4 percent of GDP.

"It's good news.. better than we were expecting. But it has to improve more than that to hit the target at 2.63 trillion pesetas, in other words 16.5 percent less than the 1995 deficit," said Carmen Hernansanz, analyst at Merrill Lynch.
Only a week ago, Spain's deficit secretary Jose Folgado told a congressional budget committee that the central government would reach the public deficit target at 3.5 pct of GDP.
But analysts see little room for improvement, even though funds from the government's privatisation plan for this year and next should help.
Merrill Lynch, for example, forecast a central government deficit/GDP at around 3.7 percent. Bank of America put its expectation at 3.9 percent and Paribas at 4.0 pct.

And the public sector budget deficit -- which is what is assessed for Europe's single currency criteria -- could be even worse, analysts said. They forecast it could be above five percent of GDP instead of the 4.4 percent target.

In the first nine months, expenditure declined 2.9 percent over the year-ago period, a level not far from the target of 3.1 percent. But at the same time revenue rose a mere 6.9 percent, in comparison with the 8.8 percent aim.
And a weaker economy raises question marks over how much the government can increase its revenues in the coming months.

"The revenues from corporate taxes are still very high, they increased 8.7 percent in the first nine months from the year-ago period, but it can't last: the economy is not growing enough," said Henrik Lumholdt, chief economist at Bank of America in Madrid.

In September, corporate taxes rose 23.7 percent in comparison with the same month of the previous year, while in the first three quarters it jumped 12 percent over the same period of 1995. Revenue from VAT taxes rose 19.4 percent at 8.7 percent respectively.
"I don't think any bigger improvement in corporate taxes or in consumption taxes before year end is really possible," Lumholdt added.
The decline in interest rates is barely influencing this year's expenditures and will have more impact next year.
"The drop we saw in interest rates during recent months will take effect only on next year's deficit," said Hernansanz.
In September, interest expenditure declined 10.9 percent, but in the first nine months had fallen a mere 0.9 pct.
But the massive privatisation process could provide a nice surprise for both 1996 and 1997, analysts said.
Up to September, Spanish government revenue from capital assets rose by 29.7 percent to 545.4 billion pesetas.
And the already planned sell-off of the 3.8 percent stake in Gas Natural could, for example, add something around 30 billion, analysts said.
-- Madrid Newsroom + 34 1 585-2160
